catalog_quote: 5. Suprasegmental phonemes. Suprasegmental features are stress, pitch, and nasalization. 5.1. Stress. All monosyllabic words are stressed: kí 'bitter manioc', tá 'grass'. Multiple stress occurs: (1) on two-syllable words, (2) on the two principal pitch pattern classes of three-syllable words, and (3) on various other three-syllable words. Stress is marked /'/ on words that do not have multiple stress. ... 'leaf', ... 'river', ... 'coca', ... 'slats', ... 'Siriano, an Indian tribe'. On two-syllable words and three-syllable words of multiple stress there is a crescendo from the first syllable to the ultimate: ... 'blowgun', ... 'deer'. Words of four or more syllables crescendo to the second or third syllable and then decrescendo: ... 'fingernail', ... 'eyebrow'. 5.2. Pitch. Drop the secondary 'LEXICAL (stress) also defensible' in favour of Ramirez 1997 sec. 3.6.1 (stress non-distinctive, emphasis-dependent, tendency to alternate every two moras); cite Ramirez sec. 3.4/3.6 as the deciding source alongside West & Welch 1967, and upgrade evidence grade to text-layer reference grammar.

sources.note: Standard reference grammar with a 29-pp. suprasegmental chapter and instrumental (CECIL) tone measurements; our coding rests on a 14-pp. 1967 SIL sketch that its own authors call a 'bare outline'. States outright that intensity stress is non-distinctive and emphasis-dependent while tone is lexical, which settles our primary TONAL code and removes the 'LEXICAL stress also defensible' secondary.
